Countess of Huntingdon
koun'tes ov hunt'ing-dūn
n. (Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, 1707–1791, patron of Calvinistic Methodism and founder of the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion)
Countess, feminine of count, from Latin comes; Huntingdon, an English county town.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon, used a peeress's rank and fortune to plant the gospel where it could not otherwise go. Converted about 1739 and widowed in 1746, she appointed Whitefield her chaplain, which under the law entitled her to maintain chapels, and she built or bought some sixty-four of them — at Bath, Brighton, Tunbridge Wells, London — places the aristocracy could attend without social cost, and where they heard the new birth preached without softening. She founded the college at Trevecca in 1768 to train preachers, sold her jewels to pay for chapels, and sent ministers to Georgia. Forced in 1781 by a consistory court to register her chapels as dissenting meeting houses, she left the established church rather than close them, and her Connexion survives. Luk 14:23 is her strategy: go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a patron as one who countenances, supports or protects; and a chapel, as a house of worship; a place of divine service.

expand to see more

PA'TRON, n. One who countenances, supports or protects; a defender; an advocate. In the church of England, one who has the gift of a benefice.

CHAP'EL, n. A house for public worship; a place of divine service, subordinate to a church.

CONNEX'ION, n. A body or association of persons united; relation by blood or marriage.

Key Scripture

Luk 14:23 — "And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled."

Jas 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Mat 5:16 — "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."

1Co 1:23 — "But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;"

Modern Corruption

She sold her jewels, built sixty-four chapels, and preached the new birth to duchesses who could not be reached any other way.

expand to see more

The strategy was not flattery of the great. Her chapels were built so that the nobility could hear Whitefield and Romaine without the social penalty of attending a meeting house, and what they heard was 1Co 1:23, Christ crucified, with no concession to rank. One duchess famously complained that the doctrine was monstrously insulting because it put her on a level with the common wretches that crawl the earth, which is exactly what the countess intended her to hear.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that wealth and position are stewardships to be spent, not platforms to be enjoyed. Jas 1:27 defines pure religion by visiting the afflicted and keeping unspotted from the world, and a peeress keeping unspotted in Georgian Bath was doing something difficult. Mat 5:16 ties visible works to the Father's glory, which is the right account of a woman whose chapels still stand.

"“to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27) — in Georgian Bath."

"“we preach Christ crucified” (1Co 1:23) — what the duchesses heard."
